analysis.one_liner: Creates an FDA pathway to approve cheaper generic copies of synthetic insulin.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2019 with 4 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Insulin has long been sold under patents at prices many patients struggle to afford, because there was no fast-track route for cheaper generic copies of the product. This bill would amend the law so the FDA could approve chemically synthesized insulin, or an analogue of it, as a generic drug through the abbreviated new drug application process, which lets a copycat drug reach the market without repeating the full clinical testing the original already proved. It would have applied to applications filed on or after January 1, 2020. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who need insulin, especially the roughly 1 in 4 insulin users who report skipping or rationing doses because of cost. Cheaper generic competition would push down the prices they pay at the pharmacy. Generic drug manufacturers would also gain a new market to enter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin-dependent patients and generic drug makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a legal pathway for the FDA to approve chemically synthesized insulin, or an analogue of it, as a generic drug under the abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) process, which skips the costly clinical trials already completed for the original product.

Generic competition is the standard way prescription drug prices fall; a generic insulin approved through this pathway would give pharmacies and patients a lower-priced alternative to brand-name insulin.
The change applies to applications submitted on or after January 1, 2020, meaning relief could have begun soon after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name insulin manufacturers, who would face generic competition for their synthetic insulin products and lose sales and pricing power. Insurers and employers might see modestly lower drug costs, while the government would forgo no direct spending under the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill routes synthetic insulin through the generic (ANDA) pathway rather than the more rigorous biosimilar pathway created for biological products, and generic approval requires less clinical testing than an original approval; a supporter would have to acknowledge the tradeoff between speed and price on one side and the depth of safety and quality review on the other.

A generic pathway addresses list-price competition but does not touch the pharmacy benefit manager and rebate system that shapes which insulin patients actually pay for, so savings at the counter could be smaller than the headline suggests.
The bill is narrow: it covers chemically synthesized insulin and its analogues only, so newer biologic insulin products would remain outside the pathway it creates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: insulin is a decades-old drug, and patients pay far more than the cost of making it because cheaper copies face regulatory barriers. The bill's design is simple and targeted, though modest in scope and dependent on generic manufacturers actually entering the market. The main cost falls on a small group of highly profitable manufacturers, which is the intended point of the policy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress; it was never voted out of committee and never reached the House floor, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) introduced the MAGIC Act on September 9, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where its House action ended.
Four House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no additional cosponsors joined after that.

The Committee on Energy and Commerce never reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without further action, so the bill received no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name insulin manufacturers came out ahead: with no law and no competing product, they kept exclusive control of the insulin market and the high prices that come with it, while patients kept paying those prices. The generic drug industry also gained nothing, since the pathway was never opened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name insulin makers kept their prices

for.name: Rep. Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a generic drug approval pathway for synthetic insulin.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never voted to send it to the House floor; its Health Subcommittee took no action after receiving the referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; the only recorded support was from five House Republicans (the sponsor and four cosponsors), and no Democrats are recorded as joining.

industries.note: The bill would have opened the market to generic copies of synthetic insulin, eroding the patent-protected pricing power of manufacturers like the three firms that dominate U.S. insulin sales. Because the bill never advanced, these manufacturers retained their exclusive market and high prices throughout.
The bill would have created a cheaper, faster approval route for generic insulin, a new market opportunity for generic makers. But the pathway never opened, so nothing changed for them.

The bill did not address how intermediaries negotiate insulin prices and rebates, so the existing structure was untouched either way. A generic entrant could have disrupted rebate economics, but no product resulted.
